myth: The ancient Egyptians were primitive people
fact: The ancient Egyptians built massive pyramids, developed hieroglyphic writing, practiced medicine, and had a sophisticated legal system.

myth: Roman gladiators always fought to the death
fact: Most gladiatorial fights ended with surrender; referees could stop fights, and death was not the primary outcome.

myth: The pharaohs built the pyramids using slave labor
fact: Evidence suggests the pyramids were built by paid skilled laborers who were well-fed and housed.

myth: Cleopatra was Egyptian
fact: Cleopatra was of Macedonian Greek descent from the Ptolemaic dynasty that ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great.

myth: The ancient Romans had no concept of hygiene
fact: Roman public baths were widespread and Romans valued cleanliness, with laws requiring waste disposal.

myth: Medieval people believed the Earth was flat
fact: Most educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was spherical, following Greek and Roman scholarship.

myth: The medieval period was a dark age of ignorance
fact: The medieval period saw the rise of universities, Gothic architecture, the printing press, and significant scientific inquiry.

myth: Knights in armor could not move or fight effectively
fact: Armored knights were highly mobile and trained to fight effectively; a suit of armor weighed about 20-25 kg.

myth: The Black Death was caused by rats alone
fact: Fleas on various mammals, including humans, spread the plague bacteria; airborne transmission also played a role.

myth: Medieval castles were always cold and drafty
fact: Castles used tapestries, fireplaces, and thick stone walls to retain heat; some had central heating systems.

myth: Christopher Columbus proved the Earth was round
fact: Educated people already knew the Earth was spherical; Columbus proved the Americas were reachable by sailing west.

myth: The Viking Leif Erikson was the first European to reach North America
fact: Viking sagas and archaeological evidence at LAnse aux Meadows confirm Norse settlement around 1000 CE.

myth: Marco Polo invented pasta and brought it to Italy from China
fact: Pasta existed in Italy before Marco Polo; his travelogue does not mention bringing noodles from China.

myth: Magellan circumnavigated the globe
fact: Magellan was killed in the Philippines; Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage with the surviving crew.

myth: Napoleon was extremely short
fact: Napoleon was about 5'7 inches, average height for a Frenchman of his era; the myth came from British propaganda.

myth: World War I was fought entirely in trenches
fact: While trench warfare defined the Western Front, fighting also occurred at sea, in the air, and on other fronts.

myth: The Trojan War is entirely fictional
fact: Archaeological evidence suggests Troy existed and was destroyed, supporting a historical basis for the conflict.

myth: Vikings wore horned helmets in battle
fact: No archaeological evidence supports horned helmets; the myth originated from 19th century romantic nationalism.

myth: The Battle of Thermopylae was only 300 Spartans
fact: The 300 Spartans were joined by several thousand Greek allies, including Thespians and Thebans.

myth: Leonardo da Vinci was just an artist
fact: Leonardo was a polymath who excelled in painting, anatomy, engineering, botany, and scientific observation.

myth: Albert Einstein failed math in school
fact: Einstein excelled in math and physics from an early age; the myth came from a mistranslated biographical source.

myth: Joan of Arc was illiterate and uneducated
fact: Joan of Arc could not read or write but was highly articulate, politically savvy, and tactically skilled.

myth: Shakespeare wrote all his plays himself
fact: Some scholars question sole authorship of certain works, though mainstream academic consensus credits Shakespeare.

myth: Genghis Khan was purely a destructive conqueror
fact: Genghis Khan established the Yam postal system, promoted religious tolerance, and fostered trade along the Silk Road.

myth: Archimedes used a mirror to set Roman ships on fire
fact: There is no contemporary evidence this actually happened; it may be a later embellishment of his legacy.

myth: Isaac Newton discovered gravity when an apple hit his head
fact: Newton observed a falling apple and began thinking about gravity, but the head-strike story is likely apocryphal.

myth: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
fact: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911, the first person to win in two sciences.

myth: Galileo was imprisoned for saying the Earth moved around the Sun
fact: Galileo was placed under house arrest and forced to recant, but he was never formally imprisoned.

myth: Da Vinci invented the helicopter and flying machine
fact: Da Vinci designed concepts for flying machines, but none were built or functional during his lifetime.

myth: King Arthur was a real historical king
fact: Historical evidence for Arthur is limited; he may be based on a 5th-6th century Romano-British war leader.

myth: The Library of Alexandria held all human knowledge
fact: The library was significant but did not contain all knowledge; much was lost gradually over centuries, not in one fire.

myth: Vikings used skulls as drinking cups
fact: This practice is not supported by archaeological evidence and likely comes from a mistranslation of Old Norse.
